{"kind":"proof","text":"Let G and H be nonabelian groups of order 21. By Sylow’s theorems, the number of Sylow 7-subgroups divides 3 and is congruent to 1 modulo 7. Hence each group has a unique, therefore normal, Sylow 7-subgroup. Write them as B=⟨b⟩≤G and D=⟨d⟩≤H.

By Cauchy’s theorem, choose a∈G and c∈H of order 3. Since B∩⟨a⟩={e}, normality of B implies that B⟨a⟩ is a subgroup of order 7·3=21; hence G=B⟨a⟩. Similarly, H=D⟨c⟩.

Because B is normal, aba⁻¹=bⁱ for some i∈(ℤ/7ℤ)×. Since a³=e,

b=a³ba⁻³=b^(i³),

so i³≡1 (mod 7). The solutions are i=1,2,4. If i=1, then a and b commute, and since they generate G, the group G would be abelian. Thus i=2 or i=4. If i=4, replace a by a⁻¹; the resulting conjugation exponent is 4⁻¹≡2 (mod 7). Therefore a may be chosen so that

aba⁻¹=b².

Likewise, c may be chosen so that cdc⁻¹=d².

Every element of G has a unique expression bʲaʳ with 0≤j<7 and 0≤r<3: existence follows from G=B⟨a⟩, while uniqueness follows from B∩⟨a⟩={e}. The analogous normal form dʲcʳ holds in H. Define

φ:G→H,  φ(bʲaʳ)=dʲcʳ.

This is a well-defined bijection. Moreover, using aʳbᵏa⁻ʳ=b^(2ʳk),

(bʲaʳ)(bᵏaˢ)=b^(j+2ʳk)a^(r+s),

where the exponents are reduced modulo 7 and 3, respectively. The identical formula holds in H because cdc⁻¹=d². Hence φ preserves multiplication. Thus φ is an isomorphism, proving that any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.","reason":"Sylow theory supplies the unique normal subgroup of order 7, and nonabelianness forces the conjugation action of an order-3 generator to be one of the two inverse nontrivial actions. After inverting that generator if necessary, both groups have identical normal forms and multiplication laws."}

{"problem": {"theorem": "Prove that any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "abstract_algebra", "proof_text": "\begin{proof}

    By Cauchy's theorem we have that if $G$ is a group of order 21 then it has an element $a$ of order 3 and an element $b$ of order 7. By exercise 2.5.41 we have that the subgroup generated by $b$ is normal, so there is some $i=0,1,2,3,4,5,6$ such that $a b a^{-1}=b^i$. We know $i \neq$ 0 since that implies $a b=a$ and so that $b=e$, a contradiction, and we know $i \neq 1$ since then $a b=b a$ and this would imply $G$ is abelian, which we are assuming is not the case.

Now, $a$ has order 3 so we must have $b=a^3 b a^{-3}=b^{i^3}$ mod 7 , and so $i$ is restricted by the modular equation $i^3 \equiv 1 \bmod 7$

\begin{center}

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|}

\hline$x$ & $x^3 \bmod 7$ \\

\hline 2 & 1 \\

\hline 3 & 6 \\

\hline 4 & 1 \\

\hline 5 & 6 \\

\hline 6 & 6 \\

\hline

\end{tabular}

\end{center}

Therefore the only options are $i=2$ and $i=4$. Now suppose $G$ is such that $a b a^{-1}=b^2$ and let $G^{\prime}$ be another group of order 21 with an element $c$ of order 3 and an element $d$ of order 7 such that $c d c^{-1}=d^4$. We now prove that $G$ and $G^{\prime}$ are isomorphic. Define

$$

\begin{aligned}

\phi: G & \rightarrow G^{\prime} \\

a & \mapsto c^{-1} \\

b & \mapsto d

\end{aligned}

$$

since $a$ and $c^{-1}$ have the same order and $b$ and $d$ have the same order this is a well defined function. Since

$$

\begin{aligned}

\phi(a) \phi(b) \phi(a)^{-1} & =c^{-1} d c \\

& =\left(c d^{-1} c^{-1}\right)^{-1} \\

& =\left(d^{-4}\right)^{-1} \\

& =d^4 \\

& =\left(d^2\right)^2 \\

& =\phi(b)^2

\end{aligned}

$$

$\phi$ is actually a homomorphism. For any $c^i d^j \in G^{\prime}$ we have $\phi\left(a^{-i} b^j\right)=c^i d^j$ so $\phi$ is onto and $\phi\left(a^i b^j\right)=c^{-i} d^j=e$ only if $i=j=0$, so $\phi$ is 1-to-l. Therefore $G$ and $G^{\prime}$ are isomorphic and so up to isomorphism there is only one nonabelian group of order 21 .

\end{proof}", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "rule_candidates": [{"id": "grp_first_iso", "name": "First isomorphism theorem for groups", "statement": "If phi: G -> H is a group homomorphism, then G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "conditions": ["phi is a group homomorphism", "ker(phi) is the kernel of phi"], "conclusion": "G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "rule_digest": "335c687d26f64e41584f1b8bc575aec9d78223b01c4821bf0056bf8533de0c19", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "grp_normal_quotient", "name": "Quotient group criterion", "statement": "If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.", "conditions": ["N is a subgroup of G", "N is normal in G"], "conclusion": "G/N is a group and coset multiplication is well-defined.", "rule_digest": "f6d458aa2e7463efeea7a535cdbe0f0f7930259cfe7f845b5350ec03454da876", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "ring_quotient_ideal", "name": "Quotient ring criterion", "statement": "If I is a two-sided ideal of a ring R, then R/I is a quotient ring with operations defined on cosets.", "conditions": ["I is a two-sided ideal of R"], "conclusion": "R/I is a ring and coset operations are well-defined.", "rule_digest": "5c419f063bbc02eba57c0943d5ecce5f2e4c1b370cbb5ad6d69c2e08c3b21835", "applicability": "unchecked"}], "draft": "Let \(G\) and \(H\) be nonabelian groups of order \(21\). By Sylow's theorems, the number of Sylow \(7\)-subgroups divides \(3\) and is congruent to \(1\pmod 7\), so each group has a unique, hence normal, Sylow \(7\)-subgroup. Write these as \(B=\langle b\rangle\le G\) and \(D=\langle d\rangle\le H\).

By Cauchy's theorem, choose elements \(a\in G\) and \(c\in H\) of order \(3\). Since \(\langle a\rangle\cap B=\{e\}\) and their orders multiply to \(21\), \(G=B\langle a\rangle\). Similarly, \(H=D\langle c\rangle\).

Normality of \(B\) gives \(aba^{-1}=b^i\) for some \(i\in(\mathbb Z/7\mathbb Z)^\times\). Because \(a^3=e\),
\[
b=a^3ba^{-3}=b^{i^3},
\]
so \(i^3\equiv1\pmod 7\). The solutions are \(i=1,2,4\). If \(i=1\), then \(a\) and \(b\) commute; since they generate \(G\), this would make \(G\) abelian. Thus \(i=2\) or \(4\). Replacing \(a\) by \(a^{-1}\) when necessary changes exponent \(4\) to its inverse \(2\pmod 7\). Hence we may choose \(a\) so that
\[
aba^{-1}=b^2.
\]
Likewise, we may choose \(c\) so that \(cdc^{-1}=d^2\).

Every element of \(G\) has a unique expression \(b^j a^r\), where \(0\le j<7\) and \(0\le r<3\). The analogous statement holds in \(H\). Define
\[
\phi(b^j a^r)=d^j c^r.
\]
This is therefore a well-defined bijection. Moreover,
\[
(b^j a^r)(b^k a^s)=b^{j+2^r k}a^{r+s},
\]
with exponents taken modulo \(7\) and \(3\), respectively. Since the identical multiplication formula holds for \(d^j c^r\), the map \(\phi\) is a homomorphism. Consequently \(\phi\) is an isomorphism, so any two nonabelian groups of order \(21\) are isomorphic.", "feedback": {"issues": [], "reason": "The proof is correct. Sylow theory yields a unique normal subgroup of order 7; Cauchy's theorem supplies a complement of order 3; nonabelianness forces the conjugation action to be one of the two nontrivial order-3 automorphisms of C7, which become the same action after inverting the order-3 generator. The unique normal forms and matching multiplication laws then establish the claimed isomorphism."}}
